titles.Root of penis & perineum: Root of the penis and perineum

clinical: Digital rectal exam
Digital rectal examination palpates the prostate through the front wall of the rectum. A hard, irregular nodule felt there raises suspicion of prostate cancer.
Fluid in the rectovesical pouch
The rectovesical pouch is the lowest part of the male peritoneal cavity, so blood, pus or tumour deposits from the abdomen collect there and can be felt on rectal examination.
Painless testicular lump
Most testicular tumours are germ cell tumours that start in the seminiferous tubules. A painless, firm lump in the testis needs prompt medical assessment.
Epididymitis
Inflammation of the epididymis causes pain and swelling at the back of the testis. In sexually active young men it is most often caused by chlamydia or gonorrhoea.
Hydrocele

A hydrocele is fluid collecting in the tunica vaginalis, the serous sac around the front of the testis. It causes painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates, meaning a light shone behind it glows through.
Cremasteric reflex
Stroking the inner thigh makes the cremaster muscle contract and lift the testis. This reflex tests the L1-L2 nerve supply.
Indirect inguinal hernia
An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, and then along the inguinal canal inside the spermatic cord into the scrotum.
Testicular torsion

Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off blood flow to the testis, causing sudden severe pain. It is a surgical emergency, because the testis is often lost if the cord is not untwisted within about 6 hours.
Urethral tear in pelvic fracture

The membranous urethra is held fixed by the puboprostatic ligaments, so it is the part most often torn in pelvic fractures. Blood at the urethral opening after a pelvic injury suggests this kind of tear.
Reflux from the bladder

The ureter enters the bladder obliquely, and this arrangement works as a flap valve that stops urine flowing back up. If the valve fails, urine refluxes up the ureter, raising the risk of kidney infection.
Benign prostatic enlargement
The transition zone enlarges with age and squeezes the prostatic urethra. This causes difficulty starting to pass urine, a weak stream and frequent urination.
Prostate cancer
About 70% of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which lies at the back of the gland and is felt on rectal examination.
Penile fracture
Rupture of the tunica albuginea during forceful bending of an erect penis causes a penile fracture. It is a urological emergency that usually needs surgical repair.
Erectile dysfunction

Erection depends on arterial blood filling the corpora cavernosa and on the tunica albuginea trapping that blood. Narrowed arteries, for example from atherosclerosis, are a common cause of erectile dysfunction.
Straddle injury
A blow to the perineum, such as a fall onto a bar, can crush the bulb of the penis against the pubic arch and tear the spongy urethra.
Bulbocavernosus reflex

Squeezing the glans or tugging a urinary catheter makes the bulbospongiosus contract. Testing this reflex checks the S2-S4 spinal segments, and loss of it suggests damage to the sacral cord or its nerves.
Klinefelter syndrome
In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) the seminiferous tubules are small and hyalinised, so sperm production fails and the testes stay small and firm.
Undescended testis
Spermatogenesis needs a temperature a few degrees below core body temperature, so a testis that fails to descend into the scrotum has impaired sperm production and a higher risk of germ cell tumour.
Kartagener syndrome

Absent dynein arms in the axoneme cause primary ciliary dyskinesia, which is called Kartagener syndrome when situs inversus is also present. The sperm tails are immotile, so affected men are usually infertile, and airway cilia fail, causing chronic chest and sinus infections.
Intracytoplasmic sperm injection
In intracytoplasmic sperm injection a single sperm is injected straight into an egg, bypassing the acrosome reaction and zona pellucida. It is used for severe male infertility.

parts.description: The pubic bone is the front part of each hip bone, with a body and superior and inferior pubic rami that meet the opposite bone at the pubic symphysis. Each inferior pubic ramus joins the ischium to form an ischiopubic ramus, and the two ischiopubic rami together form the pubic arch below the symphysis. The crura of the penis and the perineal membrane attach to this arch, and the pubic tubercle, a bony bump at the lateral end of the pubic crest, can be felt through the skin.

The rectum is the final part of the large intestine, about 12 cm long, lying in the pelvis behind the bladder, seminal vesicles and prostate, separated from them by the rectovesical (Denonvilliers) fascia. It stores faeces until defaecation, and its wall shows three transverse folds (valves of Houston). The anal canal, its last 3-4 cm, is controlled by the internal and external anal sphincters, and the pectinate (dentate) line marks where the rectal columnar lining gives way to the squamous lining of the anal canal.

The peritoneum is the thin serous membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavities and wraps most of the organs within them. In the male it drapes over the dome of the bladder and dips down between the bladder and rectum to form the rectovesical pouch, the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity, where fluid, pus or blood can collect. Deposits of tumour here can be felt on rectal examination as a firm 'rectal shelf'. The prostate and bladder neck lie below it, outside the peritoneal cavity.

The rectus abdominis is a long strap muscle running vertically on each side of the front of the abdomen, enclosed in the rectus sheath and crossed by three tendinous intersections. It arises from the pubic crest and symphysis and inserts on the xiphoid process and the cartilages of ribs 5-7, flexing the trunk and supporting the abdominal wall. Its lateral border forms the medial boundary of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, through which direct inguinal hernias push.

The urinary bladder is a hollow, muscular reservoir lying behind the pubic symphysis in the pelvis, with a capacity of roughly 300-500 mL. Its muscular wall is the detrusor, a thick layer of interlacing smooth muscle that contracts to expel urine during micturition under parasympathetic control from S2-S4. In a section its bundles are cut in many directions, giving a whorled pattern. In men the base lies in front of the rectum and seminal vesicles, and the neck rests on the prostate.

The ureter is a muscular tube, about 25-30 cm long, that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. In the pelvis it descends along the lateral pelvic wall and enters the posterolateral base of the bladder obliquely, and this oblique intramural course acts as a flap valve that stops urine refluxing back up when the bladder contracts. In the male the ductus deferens crosses over the ureter just before it enters the bladder.

The ampulla of the ductus deferens is the dilated, tortuous terminal part of the vas, lying behind the bladder and medial to the seminal vesicle, where sperm are stored before emission. Its mucosa is thrown into large, branched folds and lined by tall columnar epithelium bearing stereocilia (long, non-motile microvilli), giving a wider, more irregular lumen than the rest of the duct. It joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens on the seminal colliculus.

The corpora cavernosa are paired erectile bodies on the dorsum of the penis, lying side by side above the corpus spongiosum and enclosed by the tunica albuginea. Each is a sponge of vascular sinusoids separated by trabeculae of smooth muscle, fed by the helicine branches of the deep artery. During erection, nitric oxide from parasympathetic nerves (S2-S4) relaxes the smooth muscle, so the sinusoids fill and compress the subtunical venules against the tunica to trap blood. In sections they appear as thin-walled, endothelium-lined spaces, some blood-filled, within smooth muscle.

The dorsal arteries of the penis are paired terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery running along the dorsum of the penis. Each lies between the deep dorsal vein, which is in the midline, and the dorsal nerve, deep to Buck's (deep penile) fascia. They supply the skin, fascia and glans of the penis, and are distinct from the deep artery, which runs inside the corpus cavernosum.

The superficial dorsal vein of the penis is a vein running along the dorsum (upper surface) of the penile shaft, within the superficial fascia just beneath the skin. It drains blood from the skin and prepuce and carries it back towards the groin, where it joins the superficial external pudendal veins and then the great saphenous vein. Lying close to the surface, it is the dorsal vein most easily seen on the penis.

The ischiocavernosus is a paired skeletal muscle of the perineum that covers each crus of the penis. The crus is the attached root of each corpus cavernosum, the erectile body of the penis. The muscle arises from the ischial tuberosity and ramus, bones at the lower part of the pelvis, and inserts into the side of the crus. When it contracts it compresses the crus and slows venous outflow, helping to maintain an erection; it is supplied by the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve.

The septa of the testis are thin partitions of fibrous tissue that extend from the mediastinum testis (the fibrous core at the back of the testis) to the tunica albuginea, the tough outer capsule. They divide the testis into about 250 pyramidal lobules, each with its base against the tunica albuginea and its apex pointing towards the mediastinum. The septa also carry the blood vessels and nerves that supply the lobules.

The seminiferous tubules are the highly coiled tubes, about 0.2 mm wide, that make up most of the testis and produce sperm. Their walls hold germ cells at every stage of development, and spermatogenesis takes about 64-74 days. Sperm production needs a temperature 2-3 °C below core body temperature, which is why the testes lie in the scrotum. In cross-section each tubule is a round profile with a central lumen; germ cell tumours such as seminoma arise from these germ cells.

The mediastinum testis is the thickened posterior part of the tunica albuginea, lying along the back of the testis. It contains the rete testis, a network of channels that collects sperm from the tubuli recti (short straight tubules), and it is entered by the testicular vessels and nerves. The septa of the testis radiate outwards from it, dividing the testis into lobules.

The head of the epididymis is the expanded upper end of the epididymis, lying over the upper pole of the testis. It is made up mainly of the coiled efferent ductules, which carry sperm from the rete testis, together with the start of the epididymal duct. In a section, its efferent ductules show a saw-toothed lumen, with alternating tall ciliated cells and shorter non-ciliated cells, which helps tell the head from the uniform duct of the body.

The tail of the epididymis is the lowest part of the epididymis, lying at the lower pole of the testis. It is the main store for mature sperm, and its duct is wide and often packed with sperm in a section. Here the duct thickens and straightens into the ductus deferens, which turns sharply upwards along the posterior border of the testis.

The parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis is the serous membrane (a smooth, moist lining) that lines the inside of the scrotal wall. The tunica vaginalis is a closed sac formed from the processus vaginalis, a finger-like outpouching of the peritoneum that is carried down into the scrotum as the testis descends. At the back of the testis the parietal layer turns over to form the visceral layer, which covers the testis and is fused with the tunica albuginea.

The internal spermatic fascia is the innermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord and testis, lying deep to the cremaster muscle. It is a thin layer of connective tissue derived from the transversalis fascia, the deep lining of the abdominal wall, which is carried down around the cord at the deep inguinal ring (the entrance to the inguinal canal). It encloses the vas deferens and testicular vessels within the cord.

The external spermatic fascia is the outermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord and testis, lying just beneath the dartos layer of the scrotum. It is a continuation of the external oblique aponeurosis, the broad flat tendon of the outer abdominal muscle, and it forms around the cord where the cord emerges through the superficial inguinal ring. Beneath it lie the cremaster muscle and the internal spermatic fascia.

The external oblique aponeurosis is the broad, flat tendinous sheet of the external oblique muscle, and it forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal. Its fibres run downwards and inwards, and its lower free edge rolls under to form the inguinal ligament. Just above the pubic tubercle it splits into medial and lateral crura, which frame the superficial inguinal ring.

The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular gap in the external oblique aponeurosis, lying just above and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The spermatic cord leaves the inguinal canal through it, and its margins give rise to the external spermatic fascia that wraps the cord. Indirect hernias can bulge through it and descend into the scrotum, and direct hernias can emerge here without usually reaching the scrotum; the ring can be felt by invaginating the scrotal skin with a fingertip.

The transversalis fascia is the thin deep layer of fascia lining the abdominal wall, and it forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. The deep inguinal ring is an opening in it, and the internal spermatic fascia is drawn out from its margins along the spermatic cord. Weakness of this fascia medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, in Hesselbach's triangle, causes a direct inguinal hernia, which is common in older men and seldom enters the scrotum.

The deep inguinal ring is the opening in the transversalis fascia, lying just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament and just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. The ductus deferens and testicular vessels pass through it into the inguinal canal. An indirect inguinal hernia also enters the canal here, following the processus vaginalis, a finger-like extension of peritoneum that normally closes during infancy.

The inguinal canal is an oblique passage, about 4 cm long, through the lower abdominal wall, lying just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. It runs from the deep to the superficial inguinal ring and carries the spermatic cord in men (the round ligament in women). Its anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, its posterior wall the transversalis fascia, its roof the arching internal oblique and transversus abdominis, and its floor the inguinal ligament. The testis descends through it in the last two months of pregnancy.

The inferior epigastric artery is a branch of the external iliac artery that arises just above the inguinal ligament and ascends on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis, within the rectus sheath. It passes medial to the deep inguinal ring, and this relation separates indirect (lateral) from direct (medial) inguinal hernias. Its course puts it at risk during laparoscopic port placement.

The inferior epigastric veins are a pair of venae comitantes that accompany the inferior epigastric artery up the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis. They drain the lower anterior abdominal wall into the external iliac vein and anastomose with the superior epigastric veins above, forming a collateral route between the inferior and superior venae cavae. Their paired course alongside the artery is the easiest way to recognise them in a dissection.

Sertoli cell nuclei are pale, oval to triangular and often indented, with a large, prominent nucleolus. They lie close to the basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule, among the germ cells. Their pale, irregular outline contrasts with the rounder, darker nuclei of the germ cells, which helps tell the two apart in a section.

Spermatogonia are diploid (2n) stem cells that sit on the basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule, in the basal compartment outside the blood-testis barrier. Type A dark cells are reserve stem cells, while type A pale cells divide by mitosis to renew themselves and to produce type B spermatogonia. Type B cells enter meiosis and become primary spermatocytes, and spermatogenesis starts at puberty and continues throughout adult life.

Primary spermatocytes are the largest germ cells of the seminiferous epithelium (2n, 4c), lying in the middle of the epithelium. They spend about three weeks in the prolonged prophase of meiosis I, so their chromatin looks coarse and thread-like, and they are among the most prominent germ cells in a section. Meiosis I, the reduction division, gives two secondary spermatocytes, and errors in chromosome segregation here can produce aneuploid sperm.

Secondary spermatocytes are haploid (1n, 2c) cells formed by meiosis I, lying nearer the lumen than the primary spermatocytes. They complete meiosis II within hours, so they are rarely seen in sections, and each one divides to give two spermatids.

Spermatids are small haploid (1n, 1c) cells found close to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Round spermatids undergo spermiogenesis, a transformation without further division, in which the Golgi apparatus forms the acrosome, the nucleus condenses and elongates, a flagellum grows from the distal centriole, and excess cytoplasm is shed as a residual body. Elongating spermatids lie in deep recesses of the Sertoli cells, with their heads pointing towards the basement membrane.

Spermatozoa in the lumen are mature sperm released from the Sertoli cells by spermiation. They are still immotile, and are carried by seminiferous fluid and by contraction of the myoid cells towards the rete testis and epididymis, where they gain motility. Each primary spermatocyte ultimately yields four spermatozoa.

Germ cell nuclei change in appearance as spermatogenesis proceeds, which is how the stage of a germ cell is recognised in a section. Spermatogonia have large, rounded nuclei, and primary spermatocytes have coarse, thread-like chromatin. Early spermatids have small, round nuclei, while elongating spermatids have small, dense, condensed nuclei.

Leydig (interstitial) cells are polygonal, pink-staining (eosinophilic) cells that form clusters in the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules, usually beside capillaries. They are rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum and lipid droplets, and sometimes contain Reinke crystals (rod-shaped crystalline inclusions). Under luteinising hormone (LH) they secrete testosterone, which acts locally on Sertoli cells to sustain spermatogenesis and systemically to maintain male characteristics.

Leydig cell nuclei are round and carry a prominent nucleolus. They lie within the clusters of pink-staining interstitial cells between the seminiferous tubules, so their position as well as their shape helps to identify them in a section.

Interstitial capillaries are small blood vessels in the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules, lying close to the clusters of Leydig cells. They supply the tubules and the Leydig cells with oxygen and nutrients, and they carry away the testosterone that the Leydig cells secrete. Their endothelium lies outside the blood-testis barrier, which is formed by junctions between Sertoli cells.

The sperm nucleus forms the head of the spermatozoon and contains haploid DNA that is highly condensed, with protamines replacing histones. This compaction makes it transcriptionally silent, and the flattened head is about 5 µm long. The acrosome caps its anterior two-thirds, while the posterior third is covered only by the post-acrosomal sheath and plasma membrane.

The end piece is the short terminal segment at the very tip of the sperm tail, lying beyond the principal piece. Here the axoneme is no longer surrounded by the outer dense fibres or the fibrous sheath, so it lies directly beneath the plasma membrane, giving the tip its simple, bare structure.

The principal piece is the longest part of the sperm tail, about 45 µm long, lying between the midpiece and the end piece. Here the axoneme is surrounded by outer dense fibres and a fibrous sheath of circumferential ribs and longitudinal columns, which supports the tail. Its whip-like beating propels the sperm forward.
